system:
You extract quantitative facts about one clinical trial programme from one document.

Rules:
- Extract only facts stated in THIS document. Never use outside knowledge.
- Every fact needs "quote": an exact, verbatim span copied from the document (8-300 characters) that contains the number. Quotes are machine-checked; paraphrases are discarded.
- Placebo-adjusted values are preferred. If a value is within-arm (not placebo-adjusted), set attrs.placebo_adjusted=false.
- Units: keep the unit the document uses; put it in "unit".
- Other trials of the same investigational drug (phase 2, dose-finding, other populations, combination arms) belong
  to the programme: extract their facts too, and put the trial's name in attrs.trial when the document gives it.
- Return {"facts": []} only if the document reports no results for the investigational drug.

Allowed keys:
  n_randomized, median_followup, primary_endpoint, inclusion_threshold, planned_events, assumed_rrr, power,
  alpha, stopped_early, events_treatment, events_control, events_total, hr, ci_low, ci_high, p_value,
  biomarker_change, baseline_level, sbp_change, safety_signal, readout_statement

For biomarker_change and baseline_level, attrs must include: biomarker (one of LDL-C, non-HDL-C, apoB, HDL-C,
Lp(a), triglycerides, hsCRP, IL-6, Lp-PLA2 activity, sPLA2-IIA, SBP, other), phase (phase2 or phase3),
timepoint, method (assay or "not stated"), placebo_adjusted (true/false), dose (if stated).
For biomarker_change give "value" as the change (negative = reduction) and state in attrs.kind whether it is
"percent" or "absolute".

Return JSON only:
{"facts": [{"key": "...", "value": <number or string>, "unit": "...", "attrs": {...}, "quote": "..."}]}
prompt:
Trial: AIM-HIGH NCT00120289 - Niacin Plus Statin to Prevent Vascular Events
Investigational drug: niacin
Document: The role of niacin in raising high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to reduce cardiovascular events in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and optimally treated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol Rationale and study design. The Atherothrombosis Intervention in Metabolic syndrome with low HDL/high triglycerides: Impact on Global Health outcomes (AIM-HIGH) (journal, published 2011-02-02, source pmcid:PMC3120226)

--- DOCUMENT TEXT ---
Background To test the hypothesis that patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular (CV) disease optimally treated on a statin but with residual atherogenic dyslipidemia (low HDL-C and high triglycerides) will benefit from addition of niacin with fewer CV events compared with placebo. Statin monotherapy trials have found 25–40% CV risk reduction relative to placebo, leaving significant residual risk. Patients with atherogenic dyslipidemia have substantially increased CV risk. Methods Participants were men and women with established CV disease and atherogenic dyslipidemia. Lipid entry criteria varied by gender and statin dose at screening. All participants received simvastatin (or simvastatin plus ezetimibe) at a dose sufficient to maintain LDL-C 40 - 80 mg/dL (1.03 – 2.07 mmol/L). Participants were randomized to extended-release niacin or matching placebo. The primary end-point was time to occurrence of the first of: coronary heart disease death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome, or symptom-driven coronary or cerebral revascularization. This event-driven trial will have 85% power to show a 25% reduction in primary event frequency after 850 patients have experienced a primary outcome event. Results AIM-HIGH completed enrollment in April 2010. Follow-up is expected to continue through 2012. Summary AIM-HIGH was designed to determine whether treating residual dyslipidemia with niacin further reduces cardiovascular events in patients with CVD on a statin at target levels of LDL-C. BACKGROUND Although atherosclerotic cardiovascular (CV) disease mortality has declined significantly over the past four decades, it remains the leading cause of death and disability among men and women in the western world.1 Currently, over 13.2 million Americans have diagnosed coronary heart disease (CHD) and, despite profound advances in both pharmacologic and interventional management over the past 15 years, both morbidity and mortality remain appreciable. Elevated LDL-C is well-established as a major predictor of CHD risk and, importantly, multiple primary and secondary prevention trials with statins have convincingly demonstrated a 25–35% relative risk reduction in CHD mortality, all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and stroke; 2 however, the continuing risk for major CV events despite statin therapy remains unacceptably high, with cumulative 5-year CV event rates among statin-treated patients two
...
Early population studies have demonstrated that LDL-C elevation is not the only lipid predictor of adverse CV outcomes.3, 4 Low levels of HDL-C are also recognized as a major independent predictor of CHD risk, with a strong inverse association observed between HDL-C levels and incident CHD rates. The Veterans Affairs HDL Intervention Trial (VA-HIT) was the first study to provide some evidence that raising low levels of HDL-C in CHD patients with normal LDL-C levels was associated with significant reductions in CV events.5 An analysis of four large prospective trials demonstrated a 2–3% reduction in CHD risk for every 1 mg/dL increase in HDL-C.6 Additionally, the HDL-Atherosclerosis Treatment Study (HATS) demonstrated that treatment of the total lipid profile with a combination of simvastatin and niacin was associated with significant regression of coronary atherosclerosis and further reductions in clinical events during an average 2.5 year follow-up.7 Therapy for dyslipidemia reduces CV event frequency over periods of 3 – 8 years in rough proportion to the sum of treatment-induced percent reduction in LDL-C plus 1.3 times the percent increase in HDL-C8. Thus, for example, a 30% LDL-C decrease and 6% HDL-C increase with a statin would predict a 38% event risk reduction compared to placebo. Recent studies have focused on more aggressive LDL-C reduction strategies using high doses of statins 9 to achieve an LDL-C treatment target of ≤ 70 mg/dL in very high risk patients. Yet, in a post hoc analysis of the Treating to New Targets (TNT) Trial,10 it was noteworthy that even among those who attained LDL-C values < 70mg/dL, patients in the highest quintile of HDL-C levels had a 25% lower 5-year rate of major CV events than those in the lowest quintile (p=0.03). Moreover, the growing numbers of patients with diabetes and metabolic syndrome, characterized by the atherogenic dyslipidemia triad of low HDL-C, elevated triglycerides, and small dense LDL, present an expanding reservoir of CHD patients who are at increased risk of vascular events compared to those without metabolic syndrome.11 Despite these new insights, the evidence favoring treatment of atherogenic dyslipidemia is not considered sufficiently compelling by the National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP) to merit a recommendation for specific HDL-C goals by Adult Treatment Panel III.12 None-the-less, there is a growing evidence-based perception that treatment of atherogenic dyslipidemia will eventually become a proven adjunct to LDL-C-lowering, with a predicted near-doubling of current risk reduction13. In order to maintain the blind, placebo matching extended-release niacin contained 50 mg per tablet of immediate release niacin, sufficient to provoke a discernible flush in most patients. Those choosing to continue after the 4–8 week active run-in were given simvastatin 40 mg/day (“standard therapy”) and were randomly assigned to either extended-release niacin at 1,500 mg – 2,000 mg per day (“combination therapy”) as tolerated, or to its active placebo. For those limited to a niacin dose of 1,500 mg/day during the run-in, there was a subsequent attempt to increase dosage to 2,000 mg/day (or its equivalent placebo dose) over the first year. Protocol Clinic Procedures and Time Course: (clinic visits, phone contact, blood samples, lipid drug titration) The principal goals of the first year, which included 5 visits and 3 telephone contacts, were to teach the patient the trial expectations, to encourage long-term commitment, to assist with drug adherence, and to adjust the simvastatin dosage, with the possible addition of ezetimibe 10 mg, in order to achieve a target LDL-C in the range 40 – 80 mg/dl (1.0 – 2.1 mmol/L). Based on the LDL-C level relative to the goal range, the statin dose might remain unchanged, or doubled or halved within the dosing range of 10 mg – 80 mg. If a patient achieved an LDL-C level of 80–100 mg/dL (2.1–2.6 mmol/L) while receiving 40 mg simvastatin plus 10 mg ezetimibe, for safety reasons a dosage increase to 80 mg simvastatin plus 10 mg ezetimibe was not required. Absent symptomatic or enzymatic evidence for statin toxicity, all patients were encouraged to remain on at least 10 mg simvastatin despite very low LDL-C levels. All participants will be followed to a common termination date or death (estimated average follow-up 4.6 years; minimum follow-up 30 months and maximum approximately 7 years). Under this design, with an estimated sample size of 3,300, the trial had 99% power to detect a 25% reduction in primary outcome events among patients randomized to the combination of extended-release niacin + simvastatin (“combination therapy”), assuming a 0.089 hazard rate in patients randomized to placebo + simvastatin (“standard therapy”), using an unadjusted one-sided p-value of 0.025. Because of a lower than expected overall primary endpoint rate, protocol amendment 5, adopted April 2010, modified the primary endpoint to the expanded composite described above. The Interim Analysis Plan allows for two examinations of the efficacy data by the DSMB when approximately 50% and 75% of the projected primary events have occurred. A carotid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study has enrolled and obtained baseline MRI scans on 231 participants. An HDL proteomics/functionality and plaque inflammation substudy has enrolled 332 participants, of whom 159 are also enrolled in the MRI substudy, and will investigate the relative effects of each treatment strategy on inflammatory changes in atherosclerotic plaques and HDL particles. Of 4,275 patients entering the open label run-in, 3,414 (80%) successfully completed the run-in and agreed to be randomized. Discussion Beginning with the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study in 199414, clinical trials with statins have shown major coronary events to decrease in rough proportion to the on-treatment percent reduction in LDL-C, and overall by about 30% of the placebo-treated rates2. AIM-HIGH is the first large study to assess the clinical benefit associated with the addition of niacin to an intensive statin ± ezetimibe regimen when both groups are treated to an aggressive LDL-C target of 40–80 mg/dl (1.0–2.1 mmol/L). Niacin has been used for over 50 years in the management of cholesterol disorders.13 Niacin is most noted for its effects on HDL-C, with HDL-C increases in the 15% to 35% range. In the Coronary Drug Project, a five year, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in the 1970’s, niacin reduced the incidence of non-fatal MI by 24% and stroke by 22%, with a late benefit on overall mortality at 15 years, 10 years after the study ended.15,16 More recent imaging studies of niacin in combination with colestipol17,18 or a statin 7,19,20,21 have also consistently shown a benefit on atherosclerosis burden; however, the evidence has generally not been considered sufficiently robust to support the more widespread use of niacin or the adoption into clinical practice guidelines of therapeutic target levels for HDL-C. The mechanism of action of niacin on lipid biology is not well understood and appears to be quite complex.22,23 Niacin favorably affects levels of all lipoprotein fractions associated with atherosclerosis, decreasing apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins, including lipoprotein (a), while increasing HDL-C. These studies also show that niacin inhibitis hepatic HDL holoparticle uptake, effectively increasing the plasma residence time of HDL particles23. While fibrate-induced reduction of triglycerides is comparable to that of niacin, fibrates increase HDL-C significantly less than does niacin22. In VA-HIT5, a secondary prevention trial, gemfibrozil decreased the risk of non-fatal MI or CHD death by 22% among patients with low HDL-C (<40 mg/dL [1.0 mmol/L]) but without significantly elevated LDL-C. Gemfibrozil also decreased the risk of cardiovascular events in the primary prevention Helsinki Heart Study24; however, more recently, trials with other fibrates including BIP25 (secondary prevention, bezafibrate), and two studies among patients with diabetes (FIELD26 - fenofibrate versus placebo; and ACCORD27 - fenofibrate versus placebo on a background of simvastatin), failed to meet their primary endpoints and did not confirm a significant benefit on cardiovascular risk reduction.
